coreTruths.title: Systemic disease changes the dental plan more often than the dental treatment itself
coreTruths.broaderContext: A medical history is not paperwork. It picks up the patients in whom routine dentistry can cause bleeding, infection, drug toxicity, or cardiac events out of proportion to the procedure.
coreTruths.body:
## Three problems repeat across most systemic disease: bleeding, infection, drug handling

Whatever the diagnosis, the same three issues drive the modifications. Renal patients are a textbook example: increased risk of infection (worsened by immunosuppression), increased bleeding tendency, and reduced ability to excrete drugs [1]. Liver disease lines up similarly with bleeding risk, impaired drug metabolism, and possible hepatitis B, C, or D transmission [2]. Reading every history with these three lenses turns a long list of conditions into a short list of practical changes.

## GA is the high-risk endpoint, so most modifications aim to keep care under LA

Many medical conditions move general anaesthesia from routine to relative or absolute contraindication. Acute respiratory infections rule out elective GA in the acute phase [3]. Renal patients should never have outpatient GA [4]. Patients with liver disease should not be given GAs [5]. The pattern is the same for cardiac risk: avoid GA, especially within 3 months of an MI, use adequate LA with sedation if needed, and avoid excessive adrenaline loads [6]. So the routine answer to a complicated medical history is to find a way to do it under LA.

## Coordinate, do not improvise

When the disease is significant, the right move is liaison, not solo problem-solving. The haemophilias and Von Willebrand's disease should always be managed at specialist centres [7]. Diabetic teams, anaesthetists, and haematologists exist for exactly this reason. The dentist's job is to recognise the modifier, then loop in the right person before treatment begins.

citations.quote: ↑ risk of infection, worsened by immunosuppression. ↑ bleeding tendency. ↓ ability to excrete drugs.

The main problems presented by patients with liver disease are the potential for ↑ bleeding, inability to metabolize and excrete many commonly used drugs, and the possibility that they can transmit Hep B, C, &/or D (Hep A and E are spread by faecal–oral route).
All are C/I to elective GA in the acute phase.
Never subject these patients to out-patient GA.
Do not administer GAs.

The risk of precipitating heart failure or MI in patients with compromised cardiovascular systems is ever present. Prevent by avoiding GA, especially within 3 months of an MI, using adequate LA with sedation if necessary, and avoid excessive adrenaline loads.
The haemophilias and Von Willebrand's disease should always be managed at specialist centres. Check the patient's warning card for the contact telephone number.

coreTruths.title: Bleeding patients need a layered plan: local measures first, then drugs, then specialist input
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most bleeding problems in dentistry come from drugs and chronic disease, not rare clotting disorders. The fix is almost always local measures plus careful planning, not stopping the medication.
coreTruths.body:
## Aspirin is the commonest acquired cause of platelet trouble, and it lasts a week

Aspirin is the most common acquired cause of platelet dysfunction, and its effect is irreversible for 1 week [1]. That is a longer reach than most people remember, so any patient on aspirin gets handled like a mild bleeder for the whole week.

## A platelet count above 50 buys most of the safety margin

For anything more than a simple extraction or LA, ensure platelet levels of >50 x 109/L, preferably 75 x 109/L [2]. If active bleeding sets in, combine local measures, tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion [3]. Tranexamic acid mouthwash can reduce oral bleeding [4], and is one of the most useful additions in this situation.

## Warfarin within INR is usually safe for simple extractions

Normal therapeutic range is an INR of 2 to 4, and simple extractions are usually safe within that range [5]. Reverse warfarin with vitamin K or fresh frozen plasma if needed, but consider why the patient is anticoagulated in the first place [5]. Stopping anticoagulation to make a tooth out easier can trade a manageable bleed for a stroke or PE, which is the worse outcome.

## Liver disease and renal disease are bleeders even without a named disorder

Liver disease patients need a coagulation screen for anything more advanced than a simple extraction, and in all patients with severe liver disease [6]. They also need additional local precautions against post-operative bleeding [6]. Renal patients sit in the same camp and need additional haemostatic measures [7]. The point: bleeding risk is not limited to the haemophilia card. Read the medical history with that in mind.

citations.quote: Remember that aspirin is the most common acquired cause, its effect being irreversible for 1 week.
Management: ensure platelet levels of >50 × 109/L, preferably 75 × 109/L for anything more than simple extraction or LA.
If actively bleeding, use a combination of local measures (…… Post-operative bleeding, p. 386), tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion.
Tranexamic acid mouthwash may ↓ oral bleeding.

Given orally; effects take 48h to be seen. Normal therapeutic range is an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2–4. Simple extractions are usually safe at a level within therapeutic range. Reverse the effects of warfarin with vitamin K &/or fresh frozen plasma if needed, but consider why the patient is anticoagulated in the first place.

Take additional local precautions against post-operative bleeding following simple extractions (…… Post-operative bleeding, p. 386). A clotting screen should be obtained for anything more advanced, and in all patients with severe liver disease.
Use additional haemostatic measures (…… Post-operative bleeding, p. 386).

coreTruths.title: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis is no longer indicated
coreTruths.broaderContext: For decades dentists covered valve patients with antibiotics before invasive work. The evidence shifted, and so did the guidance. The new logic puts plaque control above pre-procedure cover.
coreTruths.body:
## Patients with rheumatic fever or valve damage do exist, but routine cover does not

Patients with a PMH of rheumatic fever very likely have damage to a heart valve, usually the mitral, and traditionally got antibiotic prophylaxis for invasive dental procedures, but more recent guidance has advised against this [1]. Murmurs still warn that damaged valves can be colonised by blood-borne bacteria, and dental procedures can cause that bacteraemia [2]. The risk has not vanished, the response has shifted.

## Prophylaxis for IE is not routine anymore

Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is no longer indicated on a routine basis [3]. The default is no antibiotic, with decisions about high-risk patients made jointly with their cardiologist rather than reflexively at the chair.

## High-risk patients still get extra care, just differently

Exception-finding still matters. Heart transplant recipients, patients with prosthetic valves or valvular damage, and those with a history of infective endocarditis may need exclusion of septic foci, and some will need dental clearances [4]. The lever is dental fitness over the long term, not a blanket pre-procedure dose.

## Where prophylaxis still applies, the principles are tight

When prophylaxis is genuinely indicated for other reasons, the regimen should be short, high-dose, and appropriate to the potential infecting organisms [5]. It should start immediately pre-operatively, less than 6 hours before, or peri-operatively, and continue for 24 to 48 hours maximum [5]. Long courses defeat the purpose by promoting resistance and disturbing commensals.

citations.quote: Patients with a PMH of rheumatic fever are very likely to have some damage to a heart valve, usually the mitral valve. Traditionally, advice has been to provide antibiotic prophylaxis for invasive dental procedures, but more recent guidance has advised against this.
They are of great relevance to dentists as their presence warns of the potential for colonization of damaged valves by blood-borne bacteria. Such a bacteraemia can be caused by dental procedures.
Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is no longer indicated on a routine basis.

Exclusion of septic foci may be requested in patients at high risk from bacteraemia, e.g. heart transplant recipients, those with prosthetic valves or valvular damage, or those with a history of infective endocarditis. It is prudent to err on the side of caution with these individuals and some will need dental clearances.

The regimen should be short, high dose, and appropriate to the potential infecting organisms. The aim is to prevent pathogens establishing themselves in surgically traumatized or otherwise at-risk tissues; therefore the antimicrobial must be in those tissues prior to damage or exposure to the pathogen. It must not, however, be present too long before this, as there is then a risk of pathogen resistance and damage to commensal organisms. The regimen should therefore start immediately pre-operatively (i.e. <6h) or peri-operatively (e.g. with anaesthetic induction) and should be continued for 24–48h maximum.

coreTruths.title: Diabetic dental care turns on insulin balance, infection risk, and timing the appointment
coreTruths.broaderContext: Diabetics show up daily and a hypoglycaemic collapse on the chair is a real risk. Most of the safe management is mundane: morning slot, food on time, antibiotic cover when warranted.
coreTruths.body:
## Hypoglycaemia is the diabetic emergency dentists actually meet

Hypoglycaemia is the diabetic emergency most likely to present to the dentist. It is acute and dangerous, and may follow a missed meal, excess insulin, or increased calorific need from exercise or stress [1]. An acutely collapsed diabetic should be assumed hypoglycaemic until proven otherwise, e.g. by blood glucose monitoring sticks or blood glucose levels [1].

## Disorientation in a known diabetic is hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise

Disorientation, irritability, increasing drowsiness, excitability, or aggression in a known diabetic suggests hypoglycaemia [2]. They often look drunk. The treatment is straightforward: oral glucose if conscious, buccal glucose gel or 1 mg IM glucagon if consciousness is impaired, IV glucose if unconscious and the kit is to hand [3].

## Diabetics are higher risk for infection and occult heart disease

These patients are more likely to have occult heart disease, renal impairment, and reduced resistance to infection, so get an ECG, U&Es, and use antibiotics prophylactically [4]. That changes the threshold for cover compared to a healthy patient having the same procedure.

## Schedule them first, in the morning, around their usual meals

Always have diabetics first on the operating list, in the morning if possible [5]. Patients under LA, or LA with sedation, should keep their carbohydrate intake and oral hypoglycaemics as normal, with surgery planned to fit their regular mealtimes and carbohydrate readily to hand [6]. Pain or trismus that disrupts eating undoes the plan, so adequate post-op analgesia is part of glycaemic control [6].

citations.quote: Hypoglycaemia is the diabetic emergency most likely to present to the dentist. It is an acute and dangerous complication of diabetes and may result from a missed meal, excess insulin, or ↑ calorific need due to exercise or stress. Most diabetics are expert in detecting the onset of hypoglycaemia themselves; however, a small number may lose this ability, particularly if changed to a new form of insulin. Recognition of this state is essential and an acutely collapsed diabetic should be assumed hypoglycaemic until proven otherwise, e.g. by blood glucose monitoring sticks or blood glucose levels.
Disorientation, irritability, increasing drowsiness, excitability, or aggression in a known diabetic, suggest hypoglycaemia. They often appear to be drunk.

If conscious, give glucose orally in any available form. Repeat if necessary every 10–15min. Get help. If impaired consciousness, give buccal glucose gel &/or 1mg of IM glucagon. If unconscious, protect airway and place in recovery position. If the correct kit is available, establish IV access and give up to 50mL of 20–50% glucose.
Remember these patients are more likely to have occult heart disease, renal impairment, and ↓ resistance to infection, so get an ECG, U&Es, and use antibiotics prophylactically.
Always have diabetics first on the operating list, in the morning if possible.

Patients being treated under LA, or LA and sedation should maintain their carbohydrate intake and any oral hypoglycaemic drugs as normal. Plan surgery to fit their regular mealtimes. Have carbohydrate readily to hand if needed, and ensure adequate post-operative analgesia, as pain or trismus can easily interfere with their usual intake.

coreTruths.title: Steroid users need cover because their adrenal axis cannot answer the stress
coreTruths.broaderContext: Long-term steroid therapy blunts the adrenal stress response. Routine dentistry usually does not need cover, but an unexpected collapse in a steroid user can kill if not recognised.
coreTruths.body:
## The longer and higher the steroid course, the more suppressed the response

Corticosteroids therapeutically or otherwise can suppress the adrenal response to stress, and the longer the course and the higher the dose, the more likely this is to occur [1]. The risk does not vanish the day the steroids stop. The window of concern stretches into the previous year.

## Cover the stress, do not chase a perfect dose

If patients have received steroids in the past year or are on steroids at present, cover any stressful procedure, anaesthetic, infection, or episode of trauma with 25 to 50 mg hydrocortisone IM (IV if under GA) 30 minutes prior to elective stress [2]. Calculating an exact dose is unnecessarily complicated and risks people forgetting, so stick to 25 to 50 mg hydrocortisone IM unless there is a very valid reason to change [2]. Plain rules win over clever ones in an emergency.

## Recognise the collapse pattern: pale, thready pulse, sudden BP drop

If collapse occurs in such a patient, the diagnosis is established by pallor, rapid thin pulse with a profound and sudden drop in BP, and loss of consciousness [3]. Treat immediately: supine, airway, oxygen, IV access, then 200 mg hydrocortisone IV and call for help [4]. Speed matters more than diagnostic certainty.

## Addison's patients need the most aggressive cover

Addison's disease is the rarest of these groups but requires the most aggressive supplementation, because sufferers are entirely reliant on prescribed steroids [5]. Minor surgery can safely be covered with IM hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100 mg qds the day of surgery, and major surgery for 3 days with the same regimen [5].

citations.quote: The use of corticosteroids therapeutically or otherwise for whatever cause may suppress the adrenal response to stress. The longer the course of Rx and the higher the dose used, the more likely this is to occur.

The prime aim is to prevent the occurrence of stress-induced collapse; therefore, if patients have received steroids in the past year or are on steroids at present, cover any stressful procedure, anaesthetic, infection, or episode of trauma with 25–50mg hydrocortisone IM (IV if under GA) 30min prior to elective stress. Seriously ill patients require IV qds doses covering the period of admission. It is a fallacy to believe you are ↓ risk of steroid unwanted effects by trying to avoid giving prophylactic steroids. Doubling the oral dose may work but is rather hit and miss. Calculating an 'exact' dose is unnecessarily complicated and risks people 'forgetting'. Stick to sticking them with 25–50mg hydrocortisone IM unless you have a very valid reason to change.
In patients presenting acutely, treat immediately. If collapse occurs in such a patient, ∆ is established by pallor, rapid, thin pulse with a profound and sudden ↓ in BP, and loss of consciousness.
Place in supine position. Maintain airway. Give O2. Obtain IV access. 200mg hydrocortisone IV immediately. Ensure help (i.e. an ambulance) is requested. Exclude other causes of collapse.

This is the rarest of these groups but requires the most aggressive supplementation as sufferers are entirely reliant on prescribed steroids. Minor surgery can safely be covered with IM hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100mg qds the day of surgery. Major surgery should be covered for 3 days using the same regimen.

coreTruths.title: Most dental emergencies follow a small playbook: airway, oxygen, supine, call for help
coreTruths.broaderContext: The set of life-threatening events in a dental practice is short. Each has a clear first move. Knowing them cold turns a panicked situation into a manageable one.
coreTruths.body:
## Fainting is the most common cause of sudden loss of consciousness

Fainting (vaso-vagal syncope) is innocuous providing it is recognised. It is easily the most common cause of sudden loss of consciousness, with up to 2% of patients fainting before or during dental Rx [1]. Treatment is mostly positional: lower the head to the level of, or below, the heart, by laying the patient flat with legs slightly elevated [2]. Most cases recover within seconds.

## Cardiorespiratory arrest: do not wait for expertise, act

Ninety per cent of deaths from cardiac arrest occurring outside hospital are due to ventricular fibrillation, which is potentially reversible by prompt defibrillation in less than 90 seconds [3]. Statistically the patient's best chance at survival once absence of breathing is confirmed is defibrillation, so getting early help may be the most useful thing to do [4]. Compressions run at 30 to 2 with a target rate of 100 to 120 per minute [5].

## Anaphylaxis: 0.5 mL of 1:1000 adrenaline IM, repeat every 5 minutes

Anaphylaxis is not all-or-nothing. It usually starts a few minutes after a parenteral injection, and the quicker the onset the more severe it tends to be [6]. The adult dose is 0.5 mL of 1:1000 adrenaline IM, repeated after 5 minutes, then every 5 minutes until improved. Do not give IV; this concentration will induce ventricular fibrillation [7]. That last bit catches people out, so it is worth memorising.

## Acute chest pain: oxygen, aspirin 300 mg PO, ambulance

For acute chest pain in dental practice: summon help, administer analgesia (nitrous oxide and oxygen in the chair), do not panic, be prepared should cardiac arrest supervene, give aspirin 300 mg PO, and tell ambulance staff what has been done [8]. Sit the conscious patient upright, since supine increases pulmonary oedema and breathlessness [9].

## Acute asthma: salbutamol, oxygen, then steroids if needed; watch for anaphylaxis in disguise

Keep the patient upright, give salbutamol by inhaler and a spacer device, repeat every 10 minutes, and give oxygen [10]. Be aware of the possibility of anaphylaxis mimicking acute asthma; remember adrenaline 0.5 mL 1:1000 IM [11]. If the patient cannot talk, the attack is potentially fatal [12].

## When the diagnosis is unclear: airway, oxygen, supine, call for help

When presented with a suddenly collapsed patient, the first thing to assess is the responder's own response. Do not panic; rational function is what makes the responder useful [13]. Maintain the airway, give oxygen, place supine; if simply fainted they recover almost immediately [14]. If breathing is normal but they do not recover, treat the common reversible causes (glucagon 1 mg IM in practice, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV in hospital) [15] while help is coming.

citations.quote: Fainting (vaso-vagal syncope) is innocuous providing it is recognized. It is easily the most common cause of sudden loss of consciousness, with up to 2% of patients fainting before or during dental Rx.
Lower the head to the level of, or below, the heart. Best achieved by laying the patient flat with legs slightly elevated.

Ninety per cent of deaths from cardiac arrest occurring outside hospital are due to ventricular fibrillation (VF). This is also the commonest arrest pattern seen in hospital. It is potentially reversible by prompt (<90sec) defibrillation.
Remember, statistically the patient's best chance at survival once absence of breathing is confirmed is defibrillation; therefore, getting early help may be the most useful thing you can do.
CPR, single and two rescuers: 30 compressions to 2 ventilations. Aim for 100–120 compressions/min.

An anaphylactic reaction is not an all-or-nothing response, and grades of severity are seen. Generally, the reaction starts a few minutes after a parenteral injection, and not immediately as does a simple faint. Some caution should be exercised, though, as the quicker the onset of an anaphylactic reaction the more severe it is likely to be.

Summon help (ambulance). Administer analgesia; the most appropriate form available here will be nitrous oxide/O2 mixture (50% O2). Don't panic. Be prepared should cardiac arrest supervene. Give aspirin 300mg PO. Tell ambulance staff what you have done.

Management depends on your immediate environment, but always ensure the patient is placed in a supported upright position if conscious, as the supine position increases pulmonary oedema and hence breathlessness.
Keep the patient upright. Administer salbutamol by inhaler and a spacer device. Repeat every 10min until resolved (or ambulance arrives). Give O2.
Be aware of the possibility of anaphylaxis mimicking acute asthma. Remember adrenaline 0.5mL 1:1000 IM.
If the patient is unable to talk, you are dealing with a potentially fatal episode.

When presented with a suddenly collapsed patient, the first thing to assess is your own response. Don't panic. You are only of value to the patient if you can function rationally. Always instigate a call for help—we are all useless without it.
Maintain the airway and provide O2 if available. Place in the supine position. If the patient has simply fainted they will recover virtually immediately.

If in dental practice, give glucagon 1mg IM. If in hospital, establish IV access and give up to 20mL 20–50% glucose IV. Give hydrocortisone up to 200mg IV. Or if unable to get access, use glucagon 1mg IM.

coreTruths.title: Pregnancy is a temporary contraindication to most of routine dentistry
coreTruths.broaderContext: The unborn fetus is sensitive to drugs, radiation, and anaesthesia, especially in the first trimester. Asking about pregnancy is a habit, not an afterthought.
coreTruths.body:
## Always ask the question

The handbook's prompt is direct: always ask whether she is, or could be, pregnant [1]. It is an easy step to forget and an expensive one to miss.

## Pregnancy contraindicates GA, most drugs, and non-essential radiography

Pregnancy is a contraindication to elective GA, the vast majority of drugs, and non-essential radiography, with the most vulnerable period being the first 3 months [2]. Elective Rx is best performed in the mid-trimester [2]. So urgent care still happens, but elective work waits, and the second trimester is the window when something has to be done.

## Migraine and the pill, and DVT and the pill, are easy reminders

The oral contraceptive is a contributing factor to migraine in many women [3]. The pill should be stopped prior to any major surgery because of DVT risk [4]. These small links matter when reading a young female history: migraine, surgery planning, and contraception belong in the same paragraph.

citations.quote: Always ask yourself: 'Is she, or can she be, pregnant?'

Pregnancy is a C/I to elective GA, the vast majority of drugs (…… Prescribing, p. 596), and non-essential radiography (the most vulnerable period being in the first 3 months). Elective Rx is best performed in the mid-trimester.
F > M, the oral contraceptive being a contributing factor.
Stop the pill prior to any major surgery.

coreTruths.title: Immunocompromised patients fail in a predictable direction: opportunistic infection that can be fatal
coreTruths.broaderContext: An immunocompromised patient does not just get more infections. They get unusual ones from organisms a normal host would shrug off, and these can kill quickly without aggressive treatment.
coreTruths.body:
## Routine procedures can become high-risk

The chief effect of being immunocompromised is increased susceptibility to infection, often due to opportunistic organisms. Anything which changes the host environment in favour of opportunistic pathogens (e.g. surgery, broad-spectrum antibiotics) can lead to potentially fatal infection with rare or otherwise innocuous organisms [1]. Routine extractions are not routine in this group.

## Some conditions look mild on paper but still increase risk

The risk gradient is not all or nothing. Autoimmune disease (e.g. SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) carries a minor increased risk of infection [2]. Diabetes mellitus is common and carries a moderate increased risk of infection [3]. All haematological malignancies severely increase risk of infection [4]. The same patient may need very different cover depending on which group they fall into.

## Treat infection aggressively, prophylax the immunocompromised broadly

Aggressive treatment of infections and antimicrobial prophylaxis are needed [5]. For a severely leucopenic patient, the example regimen is 2.25 g piperacillin/tazobactam plus 120 mg gentamicin IV pre-operatively, repeated qds for 24 hours [6]. Broad-spectrum prophylaxis is appropriate in this group, the opposite of the targeted approach used in healthy patients [7].

## In haematological malignancy, the three risks are anaemia, bleeding, and infection

In haematological malignancy, anaemia, bleeding, and infection are the overwhelming risks. Look for and treat anaemia. Avoid aspirin, other NSAIDs, trauma, and IM injections. Prevent sepsis, and if it occurs, treat very aggressively with locally recommended broad-spectrum antibacterials and antifungals, and liaise with the haematologist urgently [8]. The advice writes itself once that triad is internalised.

Autoimmune disease (e.g. SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) carries a minor ↑ risk of infection.
Common and carries a moderate ↑ risk of infection.

When practicable, select an antimicrobial as specific to the common pathogens for that procedure as possible, except in the immunocompromised, where broad-spectrum prophylaxis is appropriate.
